summary_html: Case results in **child fatality or serious injury**, triggering mandatory federal and state review. Data and lessons inform systemic reform.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — establishes national commission and reporting requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure and case review of fatalities

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of qualified immunity to state caseworkers, holding it was clearly established that children placed in state foster custody have a substantive due process right to protection, medical care and supervision.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Eighth Circuit's authority for liability when a child is seriously harmed in a state-arranged placement.
key_cases.quote: Accordingly, we affirm the district court's denial of the Defendants' motion to dismiss based upon qualified immunity.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for child-protection workers after a foster child's death, holding their conduct did not amount to the deliberate indifference required to shock the conscience.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Eighth Circuit's standard for civil liability arising from a child's death while the agency was involved.
key_cases.quote: When deliberation is practical, the officials' conduct will not be found to be conscience-shocking unless the officials acted with deliberate indifference.

key_cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Child of J.K.T.
key_cases.holding: The court held that a parent's appeal from a termination order remains justiciable after the child's death because collateral consequences attach to the order, and affirmed the termination on the merits.
key_cases.relevance: It is the published Minnesota decision addressing what survives when a child in the child-protection system dies during the case.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that collateral consequences attach to the termination order because it may affect any future termination proceedings against appellant.

key_cases.holding: Reversing the court of appeals and reinstating a wrongful-death complaint, the court held that a common-law negligence action may be maintained against a county and its child-protection workers for negligence in the investigation of, and intervention in, reports of suspected child abuse required under the Child Abuse Reporting Act.
key_cases.relevance: It arises directly from a child fatality during an open county investigation and defines the civil remedy available to the child's next of kin.
key_cases.quote: Accordingly, we hold that a cause of action can be maintained for negligence in the investigation of child abuse and neglect reports as required under CARA.

state_agency.name: Minnesota Department of Children, Youth, and Families
state_agency.hotline: No statewide hotline. Call the county or Tribal child protection agency where the child lives — the directory link is on dcyf.mn.gov/individuals-and-families/report-abuse

extended_foster_care_age: To age 21 (voluntary; youth must meet one of five eligibility conditions; re-entry to 21 allowed; Minn. Stat. § 260C.451)

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Must file TPR or document compelling reason

timeline_requirements.starts_from: The child's placement out of the home of the parent or guardian from whom the child was removed
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Minn. Stat. § 260C.204; subd. 1 requires the court to hold the permanency progress hearing no later than six months after the child's placement, and subd. 4(a)(2) lets the court continue the matter no more than six additional months before a hearing under §§ 260C.503 to 260C.521.
